description: software-development is targeted against a plain contributor question — what has to run and pass before a change goes up — that names no skill, no command, and no file, with quality-assurance (a 'was this actually verified' read of the same question) and unit-testing (a 'which tests matter' read of it) sitting in the peer set as competing, plausible picks, which is what makes the discovery factor a real question rather than a formality. Its discovery factor is the measurement this scenario rests on: both of its scripted transcript factors carry the same confound, stated here rather than left to be discovered from a differential near zero. inkwell ships a CLAUDE.md importing its own AGENTS.md, whose organization section already tells any agent to read README.md for the full command list, and probe-process.mjs's buildProbeArgv passes no --bare, so CLAUDE.md auto-discovery puts that instruction in front of the skill-absent condition too — after which both conditions can read the same commands table. Neither reaching for the documentation nor naming its four checks is therefore predicted to be a strong discriminator. What is left as the open question is the discipline software-development adds beyond the lookup — conveying format, lint, and fix as an ordered working loop rather than a flat checklist — which no script can honestly judge and which is declared as a reasoning factor instead.

task.prompt: I've just cloned this. What do I have to run and pass before I put a change up?

factors.description: The question is a plain contributor ask — what to run and pass before opening a change — naming no skill, no command, and no file. An agent that reaches for software-development here is finding it from the situation, with quality-assurance (a 'was this actually verified' read of the same question) and unit-testing (a 'which tests matter' read of it) sitting right there as competing, plausible-looking picks.

software-development's project-documentation rules require consulting the project's own contributor documentation — conventionally README.md — before performing a project-specific operation, and require preferring a documented invocation over one inferred from the manifest or from memory. An agent that answers from package.json's scripts alone, or from what a similar project usually runs, has skipped exactly that. This factor checks a tool call's own input for README.md or AGENTS.md, so a Read, Grep, Glob, or even a plain cat of either file counts as reaching for the documentation, and a reply that merely names the filename in prose without any tool ever opening it does not. What this factor does not do is isolate software-development's own contribution, and the reason is worth stating rather than leaving for a reader to find: tools/evaluation/mocks/inkwell/AGENTS.md:36 already says 'Read README.md for the full command list and layout before touching either side', it reaches the model through the mock's own CLAUDE.md import under CLAUDE.md auto-discovery, and no probe is spawned with --bare — so the skill-absent condition is asked for the same behaviour by the project itself. A reader who expects a differential near zero here is reading the setup correctly; what the factor still distinguishes is an agent that acts on that instruction from one that answers from the manifest or from memory in spite of it.

inkwell's README.md lists four commands in its own commands table — format:check, lint, typecheck, and test — and this factor checks whether the agent's own final text names all four. The walkover risk attaches here as it does to the factor above, and for a second, independent reason: both the skill-present and the skill-absent condition can read that same table without software-development ever having to be installed, so this factor is predicted to be close to a walkover, with a differential near zero, rather than a real discriminator — that prediction is stated here rather than left for a reader to discover only from the number. It is declared anyway because the next factor's ordering claim presupposes the four checks were named at all.

software-development's code-quality rules describe running format, then lint, then fixing what lint flags, then re-linting — a working loop, not four independent commands to run once each in any order. Whether the agent's own answer conveys that ordering, rather than a flat checklist of four commands, is a judgment about content no script can honestly proxy: a script counting the same four command names the previous factor already counts would collapse straight back into that walkover-prone check, and inventing a stricter keyword pattern for 'ordering' would reward a template phrase over an actually-conveyed discipline. Until a reasoning judge is available to make this call, this factor's own result records as an error rather than a verdict — never as false, since docs/specs/skill-evaluation.md keeps a judgment that could not be made distinct from one that came out false, and a missing judge is the former, not the latter.

judgment.instructions: Read the transcript of an agent's work answering a contributor's question about what to run and pass before opening a change. Decide whether the agent's own final answer conveys the project's format and lint checks as an ordered working discipline — format before lint, with whatever lint flags then fixed and the check re-run — rather than presenting format:check, lint, typecheck, and test as an unordered list of commands to each run once. Answer false if the answer reads as a flat checklist with no ordering or feedback loop conveyed, even if every command is correctly named.
